title: Reading n — converting constraints into a target complexity
summary: The 10⁸ operations-per-second rule and the table that maps n to the complexity you must hit.
note:
1. The 10⁸ rule
   • A judge does ~**10⁸ simple operations / second** in C++ (limits are 1–2 s)
   • Put n into your complexity: ≤ ~10⁸ passes, 10¹⁰ does not
2. n → target (memorise)
   • n ≤ 12 → O(n!) permutations
   • n ≤ 20–25 → O(2ⁿ) subsets / bitmask
   • n ≤ 500 → O(n³)
   • n ≤ 5000 → O(n²)
   • n ≤ 10⁵–10⁶ → **O(n log n) or O(n)**
   • n ~ 10⁹ → O(log n) or O(1)
3. Value constraints are hints too
   • values to 10⁹ and you add them → `long long`
   • small value range (letters, 0–100) → counting array
   • negatives present → sliding windows on sums break
4. In an OA
   • Write `target: O(...)` before coding; if out of ideas, code brute force for partial marks
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.q: How many operations per second should you assume?
Values up to 10⁹ and you sum them — what type?

shot.title: Constraint table
shot.body:
| n up to | Target | Typical techniques |
|---|---|---|
| 10–12 | O(n!) | permutations |
| 20–25 | O(2ⁿ) | subsets, bitmask, backtracking |
| 500 | O(n³) | triple loops, interval DP |
| 5,000 | O(n²) | 2D DP, all pairs |
| 10⁵–10⁶ | O(n log n) / O(n) | sort, heap, binary search, hashing, windows, prefix sums |
| 10⁹+ | O(log n) / O(1) | binary search on value, math |

sections.title: The 10⁸ rule
sections.body:
✍️ A typical judge does roughly **10⁸ simple operations per second** in C++. Time limits are usually 1–2 seconds.
✍️ So: plug n into your complexity. If the result is ≤ ~10⁸, it passes. If it is 10¹⁰, it does not.
Example: n = 10⁵ and O(n²) → 10¹⁰ → too slow. O(n log n) → 1.7·10⁶ → fine.

sections.title: The table
sections.body:
✍️ Learn this table by heart — it is the single most useful thing on this page.

| n up to | Target complexity | Typical techniques |
|---|---|---|
| 10–12 | O(n!) | permutations |
| 20–25 | O(2ⁿ) | subsets, bitmask, backtracking |
| 100 | O(n⁴) | brute force over 4 indices |
| 500 | O(n³) | triple loops, interval DP, Floyd–Warshall |
| 5,000 | O(n²) | 2D DP, all pairs |
| 10⁵ – 10⁶ | O(n log n) or O(n) | sorting, heaps, binary search, hashing, windows, prefix sums, greedy |
| 10⁹ and beyond | O(log n) or O(1) | binary search on value, math |

sections.title: Value constraints matter too
sections.body:
✍️ Values up to 10⁹: a sum of two fits in `int` barely (2·10⁹ > 2³¹−1 ≈ 2.147·10⁹ — it does NOT). Sum of many → `long long`. See [[cpp-integer-overflow]].
✍️ Small value range (e.g. 0–100, lowercase letters) → counting arrays instead of maps; sometimes counting sort.
- Negative values → windows on sums break ([[sw-monotonicity-requirement]]).

sections.title: How to use it in an OA
sections.body: ✍️ Before coding, write `target: O(...)` at the top of your paper. If your idea is slower, do not code it yet — unless you are out of ideas, in which case code the brute force for partial marks and keep thinking.

used_by.why: Turns n into a target complexity before you think of an idea.
